This mimics HA's pattern of putting state directly adjacent to the title in tile cards. - Notice the cause/effect inversion in the **Disabled** row: with current placement, the off-switch and the resulting "Disabled" status sit visually adjacent; the eye reads cause → effect. With top placement, you read "Disabled · Slot is disabled by user" *first* and then have to scan down to find the toggle that produced it. For Inactive, the same thing happens with Conditions (effect at top, cause far below). - Heuristic: top placement wins for **read-mostly** cards (dashboards, monitors); current placement wins for **use-mostly** cards (editing, configuring). This card edits name, PIN, enable toggle, and condition entities — it's use-mostly, which slightly favors keeping status where it is. `─────────────────────────────────────────────────` My lean: **keep B's current placement**. The status sits between the things that change it (Primary Controls above) and the things that block it (Conditions below) — that's a meaningful causal middle, not arbitrary. Top placement would be the right call if this were a passive monitoring card, but you can edit almost everything on this card, so cause-and-effect adjacency wins. That said, top placement is a perfectly defensible choice if you weight scannability higher than causal proximity.

## First principles for this card Stepping all the way back. Six principles I'd hold this card to: 1. **Hierarchy follows attention.** The most-asked question deserves the most pixels and the earliest position. The card titled "Code Slot N" exists because users are asking *one* question more than any other — what is the most-asked question? 2. **Co-locate cause and effect.** If something is broken, the fix should be reachable without scanning. Cause/effect splits across the card create eye-tracking work. 3. **One canonical surface per fact.** Currently, "this slot is inactive" appears in three places (Status section text, Conditions ✗ 1/2 badge, condition row content). Pick one *summary* surface and one *detail* surface. 4. **Eliminate redundant labels.** A section called "STATUS" inside a card titled "Code Slot N" double-frames. A section called "Primary Controls" tells you nothing — primary to what? 5. **Group by user journey, not by data model.** The current sections (Primary Controls, Status, Conditions, Lock Status) match the LCM data shape. They don't match how users move through the card. 6. **Progressive disclosure for diagnostic depth.** Glanceable info above the fold; diagnostic detail one click away. The card should be useful when collapsed *and* when expanded. ## Audit of the current card | Principle | Current card | |---|---| | Hierarchy follows attention | Title "Code Slot 1" is the most prominent thing — but the most-asked question is "is Alice's PIN working?". Title is bureaucracy, not identity. | | Co-locate cause and effect | Disabled state and the toggle that causes it sit ~30px apart (good). Inactive state and the failing condition sit ~150px apart (poor). | | One canonical fact surface | Status text + Conditions badge + Condition row each restate "blocked by conditions" three times. | | Eliminate redundant labels | "STATUS", "Primary …

But the inconsistency is actually **load-bearing** — each element has a different relationship to the slot: - **Helpers** are *passive context* — "here are some entities you wanted to see alongside this slot." HA entity rows are perfect: just show me the state, let me click for more info. - **Condition entity** is the *gate* — its purpose isn't "show me this entity's state", it's "is this gate currently allowing or blocking?" The custom rendering exists to translate raw entity state into the LCM framing. - **Locks** are the *destination* — the whole reason the slot exists. what is the command to create a tunnel from a local port x to remote port x on an ssh remote host

> AGENT

``` ssh -L X:localhost:X user@remote-host ``` `-L` is local forwarding: any connection to `localhost:X` on your machine gets tunneled through SSH and emerges on `remote-host` as a connection to `localhost:X` (from the remote's perspective). Variants: - **Background, no shell:** add `-N -f` → `ssh -N -f -L X:localhost:X user@remote-host` - **Different remote target:** `ssh -L LOCAL_PORT:REMOTE_HOST:REMOTE_PORT user@jump-host` (forward to a host the remote can reach, e.g. `ssh -L 5432:db.internal:5432 user@bastion`) - **Reverse direction (remote → local):** `-R` instead of `-L` — exposes your local port on the remote - **Stay alive:** add `-o ServerAliveInterval=60` if the tunnel keeps dropping

> AGENT

That's the answer. PINs are crossed out (`text-decoration: line-through`) when the `.lcm-code.disabled` class is applied — which happens for slots where: - The lock currently has **no PIN** on it (empty/null `slot.code`) - BUT the LCM slot has a `configured_code` or `configured_code_length` in its config So the cross-out means: **"this slot is configured with a PIN, but the lock doesn't currently have it"** — typically because the LCM slot is disabled (Enable toggle off) or otherwise blocked, so the code hasn't been pushed/has been removed from the lock. The visual semantics: "there's a PIN here in theory, but it's not active on the lock." A user sees the masked dots (so they know a PIN is configured) with a strikethrough (so they know it's not currently usable). Logic is in `_getCodeClass` at `ts/lock-codes-card.ts:609-625`. Style is in `lcmCodeStyles` at `ts/shared-styles.ts:150-153`. This is pre-existing behavior, not introduced by Phase 2. Want any change to it (e.g., different visual cue, or only strike when explicitly disabled vs blocked)?

> DEVELOPER

I wonder if it should get some other type of treatment. What would a designer recommend

> AGENT

Strikethrough is semantically wrong — it means "deleted/invalid" but the PIN is just **not currently on the lock**. It also looks broken on `••••` dots (the strike doesn't have proper characters to bisect). `★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────` - The state being represented is actually two states collapsed into one: **(a) intentionally off** (slot's Enable toggle is off — PIN exists in config but admin disabled it) vs **(b) pending sync** (slot is enabled but the lock hasn't received the code yet, e.g., during a sync error or before first push). Treating them identically loses information the user needs to act on. - HA's design language for "not currently active but exists" is usually heavy dimming + a status hint (icon or word). It almost never uses strikethrough — that's reserved for things like deleted Lovelace cards or toggled-off automations in the trace UI. - The lock-codes-card already has the data to disambiguate (`slot.enabled === false` vs sync status). Currently it doesn't use it; the strikethrough is a single visual for both cases. `─────────────────────────────────────────────────` **My recommendation:** Drop the strikethrough. Replace with two distinct treatments based on cause: - **Intentionally off** (slot disabled by user): show `••••` in `--disabled-text-color` (heavily dimmed) with a subtle muted-background pill. No strikethrough. The visual reads as "exists but turned off" rather than "removed." - **Pending sync / out-of-sync**: show `••••` in `--secondary-text-color` with a small `⏱` (clock) prefix or the existing sync-pending icon. Communicates "in progress" without negativity. Both fall back gracefully if the data doesn't tell you which case applies — default to the "off" treatment. If you want the lightest-touch fix without the disambiguation: just remove the `text-decoration: line-through` and lean on color contrast alone. The dim secondary text already reads as "not the active code." That's a 1-line change you could ship today; the …

should the name get a title NAME?

> DEVELOPER

should the name get a title NAME, everything else on the card seems to

> AGENT

No — the name is the **identity** of the slot, not a labeled field. Other elements get labels because they're values within a context (PIN belongs to the slot; CONDITIONS lists what gates the slot; LOCK STATUS shows where the slot is synced). Their labels disambiguate "which thing am I looking at?" The name has no such ambiguity. It's the title of the card. Adding `NAME` above "test" would be like writing `TITLE: My Document` at the top of a Word doc — the position and prominence already communicate what it is. Compare with the kicker (`SLOT 10 · TEST`): that's not a label for the name, it's secondary context (which slot, which integration). If anything, the issue is the *name lacks an obvious "this is editable" affordance* — the pencil button is the cue. If you want the field to feel more like a labeled property (consistent with PIN), the right move would be to demote the name out of the title position entirely and put it inside the hero row alongside PIN: ``` NAME test ✎ PIN •••• 👁 Enabled ● ``` That would make all editable fields visually parallel. Trade-off: the card loses the personable "this is Alice's slot" identity at the top, becoming more form-like. The current design (name as title, others as labeled fields) is the more common pattern for entity-like cards in HA. I'd leave it. But if the asymmetry bothers you, the form-like layout above is the consistent alternative.

> DEVELOPER

as a designer, how would you reduce the vertical size of the slots in the lock card while maintaining fidelity of information?

> AGENT

The lock card shows N slots at once — the labels that work on the slot card (one focused slot) become repetitive noise here. Same `NAME` and `PIN` text on every chip is information the user has to filter past on every glance. `★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────` - Labels disambiguate fields where the user might be uncertain what they're looking at. On a multi-slot list, position and typography do that job better than text — the user sees "rows of slots" once and the pattern is set; repeating "NAME" / "PIN" on every chip is noise. - The visual parallelism with the slot card doesn't require literal labels — it requires consistent treatment. Name = bold primary text, PIN = monospace dots. Those typographic conventions are recognized without needing to be named. - Lock cards typically expand vertically with the number of slots; reducing per-chip height has compounding effect. Saving 20px per slot saves 200px on a 10-slot lock. `─────────────────────────────────────────────────` **My recommendation:** drop the NAME/PIN labels on the lock card; let position and typography carry the meaning. Keep the labels on the slot card (one focused slot — labels are useful context). The layout becomes two rows per chip: ``` Slot 5 · House Locks [Active] [Managed] Alice •••• 👁 ``` Saves ~30-40% vertical space per chip. All the same information; nothing hidden. If you want even tighter, the most aggressive move is **single-line per chip**: ``` [5] Alice · House Locks · Active · Managed •••• 👁 ``` But that breaks the chip-as-card visual language and starts feeling table-like. The two-row version preserves the chip feel while still being substantially tighter. Want me to apply the two-row version?

> DEVELOPER

I wonder, is there any value in having the condition be collapsed if the condition is applied? What would you tell me as a designer?

> AGENT

There's value in collapsing when the condition is **passing** (Active state). The user opening the card already saw `✓ Vacation calendar` in the summary badge — that's all the confirmation they need. Expanding by default just adds visual weight to a "things are fine" state. But when the condition is **blocking** (Inactive state), the user is almost certainly opening the card to figure out *why* their PIN doesn't work. Hiding the cause behind a click is friction at exactly the moment they need it. `★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────` - The principle is "show what matters when it matters". The condition section's value isn't constant — it's high-value when blocking, low-value when passing. Defaulting to expanded-when-blocking matches that asymmetry. - This is a standard dashboard pattern (e.g., HA's notification panel auto-expands errors but stays compact for info). It's not surprising once users see it once. - The user can still toggle either direction manually — auto-expand sets the default, doesn't lock it. `─────────────────────────────────────────────────` **My recommendation:** auto-expand the Condition section by default when the condition is blocking (slot Inactive). Keep collapsed by default when passing (slot Active) or when slot is Disabled (condition is irrelevant if the slot is off entirely). The empty state (no condition) stays as the static non-expanding row we already have. This is a one-line change in `setConfig` or `_renderConditionsSection` — just compute initial expansion based on `active === false`. Want me to apply it?

> AGENT

The bug is `align-items: center` on `.slot-top` — when badges stack to two rows, the slot label centers against the middle of the stack (so it visually sits *between* the two badges). In the empty chip with only one badge, label and badge align perfectly. The user prefers that — fixable by aligning the label to the top of the badge stack. `★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────` - This is a classic flex-alignment pitfall: when one child has variable height (the badge stack), `align-items: center` produces visually different positions for the other child as the variable child grows. The fix is to anchor to a stable edge (start) so the label's position is independent of badge count. - Aligning to the top also matches the conventional reading order — labels (identifiers) typically sit at the top-left, with secondary metadata (badges) flowing below or to the right. Centering inverts that hierarchy. `─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

★ Insight ───────────────────────────────────── In Lit, standard HTML attributes (`title`, `role`, `tabindex`) get type-checked against `HTMLElement`'s string-typed properties — so `nothing` (a unique symbol) fails the type check even though it works at runtime. `ifDefined(undefined)` is the typed escape hatch: the directive returns a value compatible with the attribute's expected type, but at runtime it removes the attribute entirely. `aria-*` attributes and `@event` listeners don't have the same strict typing in Lit, which is why those `: nothing` arms work fine. ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

Both PRs are up: - **PR #1118** — `generate_pin` service: https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1118 - **PR #1119** — TS attribute typing fix + slot-card typing cleanups + TODO.md trim: https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1119 ★ Insight ───────────────────────────────────── A subtle bit of Lit ergonomics worth keeping in mind: `nothing` and `ifDefined(undefined)` look like alternatives, but they target different layers. `nothing` is a runtime sentinel that Lit's renderer recognizes; it's typed as a distinct symbol, so it only fits in slots whose types are loose (event handlers, `aria-*`, child positions). `ifDefined` is a directive whose return type is structurally compatible with the attribute's expected string type — that's what makes it the right tool for typed HTML attributes like `title`/`role`/`tabindex`. Same effect at runtime, very different shape to the type system. ───────────────────────────────────────────────── The one remaining unstaged item is `.devcontainer/devcontainer-lock.json` (untracked) — left it alone since it's unrelated to either PR.
